items.headline: Moderna vaccine, Genentech obesity deal, Trump’s FDA pick — a BioCentury podcast
items.preview: Moderna and Merck's Phase III melanoma win validates mRNA neoantigen vaccines. Genentech partners with Hanmi for obesity treatment.
items.article:
A Phase III melanoma win gives Moderna and Merck important validation for mRNA neoantigen vaccines and raises the prospect of a new oncology treatment modality, but key questions remain about durability, scalability, cost, reimbursement, and applicability beyond PD-1-responsive tumors.
Roche and Genentech's Hanmi deal adds a potential first-in-class urocortin 2 asset designed to reduce fat while sparing lean mass, underscoring how large companies are diversifying beyond GLP-1s to build next-generation combination obesity franchises.
Why this matters: These developments highlight significant advancements in cancer treatment and obesity management, indicating a shift towards innovative therapeutic approaches in these fields.

items.headline: FDA extends review of Capricor cell therapy; Pain drug startup to go public
items.preview: Capricor's Duchenne muscular dystrophy therapy review extended by FDA. GSK's hepatitis B drug approved in Japan.
items.article:
The Food and Drug Administration has extended its review of an experimental Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy from Capricor Therapeutics. The agency had an Aug. 22 deadline to decide whether to approve Capricor’s deramiocel for a deadly heart-related complication of Duchenne. The FDA deemed updated application information a 'major amendment' and delayed its decision by three months, now expected by Nov. 22.
GSK has won the first clearance of a hepatitis B drug, Hibsago, approved in Japan, which is positioned as a 'functional cure' for chronic hepatitis B infections. Meanwhile, Ambros Therapeutics will go public through a reverse merger with Werewolf Therapeutics, focusing on a pain medication in late-stage testing.
Why this matters: These developments reflect ongoing advancements in therapies for serious conditions and the evolving landscape of biotech financing.

items.headline: Living Cellular Assemblies Offer New Therapeutic Possibilities
items.preview: A review discusses cellular assemblies as a new class of living therapeutics for disease treatment.
items.article:
A new review in Nature Reviews Bioengineering presents cellular assemblies as a potential new class of 'living therapeutics'—biological systems built from organized groups of cells rather than from isolated cells delivered as a suspension. Researchers hope to develop therapies that can sense disease-related conditions and coordinate complex responses.
The review examines how cellular assemblies can be designed from individual cells to larger structures, emphasizing the importance of spatial relationships in influencing function. These assemblies may provide more robust tissue repair and immunomodulation capabilities compared to traditional cell therapies.
Why this matters: This innovative approach could revolutionize regenerative medicine and therapeutic strategies by enhancing the effectiveness and longevity of cell-based treatments.

items.headline: AdaG-Net: A Multimodal Model for Mortality Prediction in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
items.preview: AdaG-Net is an AI model designed to predict mortality in ARDS using multimodal clinical data.
items.article:
A study introduces AdaG-Net, a multimodal artificial-intelligence model designed to predict mortality in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). This model combines various clinical information types to improve prediction accuracy, utilizing attention mechanisms and adaptive gating.
AdaG-Net aims to assist intensive-care teams in identifying patients needing closer monitoring and could help in evaluating new therapies. Internal validation of the model is crucial to ensure its reliability across different clinical settings.
Why this matters: This innovative approach to mortality prediction in ARDS could enhance patient care and outcomes in critical care settings.

items.headline: Metabolic and developmental rate divergence in Drosophila underlies evolutionary innovation
items.preview: Research reveals how metabolic changes in Drosophila contribute to evolutionary innovations.
items.article:
A study investigates the genetic mechanisms behind the evolution of the Drosophila sex comb, a male-specific trait. The research shows that changes in the character identity network (ChIN) lead to metabolic and developmental rate divergences between homologous cells, facilitating the evolution of new traits without the need for new genes.
The findings suggest that morphological innovation can arise from metabolic-driven differences in developmental rates, providing insights into how evolutionary processes can generate novel biological functions.
Why this matters: Understanding these mechanisms enhances our knowledge of evolutionary biology and the development of new traits across species.
